AlternateTargets: stand with one’s feet on firm earth
Senses.Note: Four direct deployments in four independent works establish the phrase as a demand for grounded, firsthand engagement.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (M/M59/M59n1540.xml). General Discourses of Chan Master Dahui Pujue. Dahui Zonggao says that entering this sort of gate is when one first plants the feet on solid ground and pulls out birth and death by the roots.

Senses.Explanation: To have the feet planted on solid ground is to answer or investigate from firm, firsthand footing instead of relying on verbal display. Chan masters use the bodily image for an actual place to stand and for inquiry that does not float in borrowed explanation. Caoshan Baoji Xiong gives the phrase as the student’s place for settling life. Tianmu Mingben tells an inquirer to discard memorized sayings and investigate with feet on solid ground. Yuanwu Keqin contrasts such a person with an interlocutor left speechless by Muzhou. Dahui Zonggao uses the phrase for entering a demanding gate that uproots birth and death.
